paragraphs: The European Union on Sunday condemned an attack by masked Israeli settlers on a convoy carrying European diplomats in the occupied West Bank, according to Al Jazeera. The attack happened Saturday near the Palestinian village of Taybeh, east of Ramallah. Diplomats from France, Belgium and Poland, along with representatives of the Catholic Church, were visiting to show support for Palestinian olive growers.

Bernard Baudoux, the 78-year-old mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries in northern France, told Reuters he was thrown to the ground. Al Jazeera reports he said he was kicked and beaten despite wearing his ceremonial sash. A window of a Belgian diplomatic vehicle was smashed. Belgium said its personnel were safe, and Poland said its diplomats were unharmed and there was no indication they were specifically targeted. The EU said it expected "full accountability" and called on Israel to stop expanding settlements.

Israeli responses differed in emphasis. Foreign Minister Gideon Saar condemned the violence, called the perpetrators rioters and said police had opened an investigation. He also criticised the delegation for not coordinating its visit with the Israeli military. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office said violence against diplomats was unacceptable but questioned whether online video established what happened. The Guardian quotes the office as saying the images "do not establish the complete sequence of events or individual responsibility."

The Guardian, whose team was in Taybeh, said it filmed the moments before the assault. It reported that video metadata showed 22 seconds between footage of Baudoux remonstrating with his attackers and footage of him on the ground, and that settlers struck the vehicle as it drove away.

The attack followed Friday's assault on US photojournalist Heidi Levine near Ramallah. US Ambassador Mike Huckabee called it a "despicable act of terror" and demanded prosecutions. The UN humanitarian office said nearly 200 settler attacks tied to this year's harvest had caused casualties or damage, already above last year's 185.

The Gulf Cooperation Council on Sunday condemned repeated attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi fighters on Saudi Arabia and pledged support for the kingdom, according to Al Jazeera. The six-member bloc, which includes Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, issued its statement after a foreign ministers' meeting in Manama, Bahrain.

The statement said an attack on any member affected all six, invoking a joint defence agreement and backing Saudi Arabia's right to protect itself. The ministers accused the Houthis of deadly strikes on civilian airports and vital facilities. They pressed for tighter enforcement of a UN arms embargo and urged countries to designate the group a terrorist organisation. They also welcomed an October 15 UN Security Council statement condemning Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia and threats to Red Sea shipping.

The Saudi-led coalition said it shot down two drones near Riyadh and in the Eastern Province early Sunday, and intercepted another near the capital hours earlier without saying who launched it. Yemen's internationally recognised government separately wrote to the UN secretary-general and Security Council, citing an attack on the presidential palace in Aden, where it is temporarily based.

On the ground, the Yemeni military said the Houthis fired missiles toward Marib, while government troops reported gains in Taiz. Government-aligned commanders said eight soldiers died in Lahij on Saturday and claimed to have killed 12 Houthi fighters in southern Taiz, figures that could not be independently confirmed. This phase followed Houthi gains along the Red Sea coast last month and a government counteroffensive.

The International Organization for Migration said the fighting has uprooted more than 233,000 people, about 121,000 of them in Taiz province. Al Jazeera reported that cooking gas was unavailable there and food prices had risen fivefold, according to a local office tracking the siege. The World Health Organization warned that Taiz's 12 hospitals had fuel for four more days and had run out of surgical supplies, amid a cholera outbreak.

Taiwan said it confronted and drove away 16 Chinese coastguard, research and fishing vessels that it described as taking part in simultaneous "maritime harassment" operations, according to Al Jazeera. The Taiwanese coastguard said in a statement on Sunday that an "unusually large" number of Chinese vessels took part in coordinated operations around Taiwan's main island and Pratas, also known as Dongsha, a disputed island to the southwest.

The Chinese vessels included four fishing boats, whose simultaneous operations the coastguard called "hybrid warfare." It said its vessels took "forceful action immediately to effectively neutralise the threats." The coastguard also accused Beijing of "attempting to unilaterally alter the status quo" in the Taiwan Strait and of trying to give a "false impression of jurisdiction." Some of the vessels reportedly entered Taiwan's restricted waters. The report did not include a response from Beijing to this particular claim.

Beijing claims both Taiwan and Pratas as Chinese territory and asserts jurisdiction over the surrounding waters, which Taipei rejects. China has long threatened to use force to gain control of Taiwan.

The report points to a run of earlier incidents. On October 1, Taiwan's coastguard fired water cannon at a Chinese recreational fishing vessel near Pratas. Taiwanese official data show Beijing deployed a record 244 coastguard, scientific research and other ships around Taiwan's main island in July, compared with 58 in the same month last year. In the first 21 days of August, 152 vessels were detected, most from the Chinese coastguard, with fishing boats and research vessels also involved.
Al Jazeera noted that China also sends warships around Taiwan on a near-daily basis, but those are counted separately from the figures above.

Anthropic announced it is creating a "public benefit fund" that it says will give the company "increased flexibility and scale" to support projects for societal good, according to TechCrunch. The company said it will commit 5 percent of its shares to the fund, which is structured as a wholly owned entity within the company. It can contribute an additional 2 percent for every 50 percent increase in Anthropic's value.

Anthropic offered broad ideas for how the money might be used, including "large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations." It also pointed to AI's possible effect on jobs, which it has already committed $200 million to study, saying "bolder approaches may be needed." TechCrunch noted that who will decide what gets funded is unanswered. Anthropic said it will share more on structure and governance in the coming months. The announcement comes as the industry faces negative public sentiment, which CEO Dario Amodei has called "fundamentally a crisis of trust."

Separately, the Financial Times, in a piece carried by Ars Technica, reported that Anthropic has granted outside evaluators "employee-like access" to assess the risks of its models. METR, a nonprofit, now has six employees embedded at the company with access to hardware and internal systems that Anthropic said are roughly on par with its own risk assessment teams.

Anthropic said it is not paying METR, and METR does not accept donations from AI companies. The evaluators will publish their analysis and Anthropic cannot veto publication, though it can require redaction of categories such as customer data, attorney-client privileged material and model architecture details. Critics cited in the report argue such arrangements could create conflicts of interest and that more government regulation is needed. The report said Anthropic is also under pressure to reassure investors ahead of an expected initial public offering.

The No Kings coalition's Instagram account went dark for several hours on Saturday while its latest nationwide protests were under way, according to The Guardian. The demonstrations focused on increasing early voter turnout, and the outage prompted organizers to voice fears of censorship.

Meta apologized on Saturday and attributed the suspension to an automated action triggered when accounts "post, share or comment at very high frequencies." Spokesperson Andy Stone wrote on X that the action "was clearly taken in error" and that everything was working again. The coalition said on Sunday it had regained access but that "Meta still owes us an explanation," adding that "restricting communications about voting in the middle of an election is unacceptable." Organizers said they were skeptical of the explanation, saying members "posted only a handful of times and livestreamed to thousands." Senator Bernie Sanders wrote on X that "billionaire ownership of the media" had led to the suspension.

Hundreds of planned events went ahead. At the Lincoln Memorial, a few hundred people gathered with signs reading "VOTE EARLY" and "HANDS OFF MY VOTE!" In Atlanta, city councilman Michael Julian Bond urged the crowd to use the power to vote. In Los Angeles, marchers called for abolishing ICE and passing California's billionaire tax, according to the New York Times as cited by the Guardian.

The Guardian said the movement began last summer in response to concerns about federal layoffs, immigration enforcement and foreign wars, and typically leans into anti-Trump sentiment. It said this year's voting focus is partly due to the Supreme Court's rollback of the Voting Rights Act and fears that Trump may question election results without basis. Organizers said they plan to recruit volunteers in case of "election sabotage."

A 34-year-old woman arrested after driving a pickup truck onto soccer fields in Wichita, Kansas, on Saturday has been released without charges while the investigation continues, according to The Guardian. Two people died: six-year-old Cole Adrian and Nicholas Schafer, 35, both from McPherson, Kansas. Police said they were not related.

In a statement Sunday, Wichita police said investigators are awaiting toxicology results and a mechanical examination of the truck. Police said they released the driver after consulting the Sedgwick County district attorney's office. They said no charges have been filed and investigators are working to determine what led to the crash. The woman, from Garden City, Kansas, had a valid license and no outstanding warrants, police said. She had two of her children in the truck, and a third was playing soccer elsewhere at the complex. The two children were among more than 30 witnesses interviewed.

Police said the driver was parked at the Stryker Sports Complex in northeast Wichita when she drove onto the fields at about 3:25 p.m. Ten other people were hurt, including five children, with injuries described as traumatic but not life-threatening. An 11th person, a 61-year-old woman, had medical complications unrelated to traumatic injuries.

McPherson City FC, a youth club, called the event "an unimaginable tragedy" and asked for privacy. McPherson's city government said the community was hurting. Police Chief Joe Sullivan said officers will keep working to understand exactly what happened.

The complex cancelled all events until further notice. The Kansas State High School Activities Association suspended its flag football third-place and championship games and said it would announce rescheduling details Monday.

The captain of the flydubai flight that was attacked by a co-pilot has described blocking axe blows to his head and screaming for help, according to The Guardian. Capt Smit Machchhar spoke to The National newspaper from a hospital bed in Abu Dhabi, his head and left arm bandaged.

Machchhar has been hailed as a hero for helping avert disaster on flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv last month. The UAE attorney general has said the co-pilot carried out an attempted suicide attack and intended to crash the plane into Ben Gurion airport. UAE prosecutors said, after a criminal investigation launched on October 1, that the plan was inspired by the September 11, 2001 attacks on the United States.

Machchhar said that when the first blow landed he thought something had gone "horribly wrong with the aircraft structure," before realizing he was being attacked. "My immediate action was to free myself from the seatbelts and I tried to just block the blows as much as I could," he said. He said the blows were coming on his head, that his hand went to the knob that opens the door, and that he screamed for his colleagues. He believes that was when he first lost consciousness.

The plane was in Saudi airspace when the co-pilot attacked with a crash axe, an item typically kept in the cockpit for emergencies. The airliner dropped 16,000 feet in 30 seconds before the attacker was overwhelmed, and two other pilots on board landed the aircraft safely in Saudi Arabia. The suspect, an Omani national, was transferred to the UAE.
Machchhar said the scariest moment was feeling the nose go "steeply down." "I was not very sure that I'll make it out alive from this," he said. "Did I give up? No."

Rep. Ritchie Torres, a New York Democrat who represents the Bronx, introduced the Power To The Players Act this week, according to The Verge. If passed, it would direct the Federal Trade Commission to write rules guaranteeing that consumers own a game when they pay for it, rather than holding a license to play it.

The bill would also require developers to put in place an offline mode before shutting down supporting servers. The Verge noted that many games now need a server connection, so they can become unplayable when a company ends server support. Torres cited NBA 2K25, which 2K will delist from storefronts at the end of the month and shut down servers for on December 31. "A game that can be taken away the moment a company pulls the plug is not a purchase," Torres said. "It is a rental disguised as a sale."

The Verge linked the concerns about ownership to Sony's announcement that it plans to phase out physical game discs in 2028. It also compared the bill to Pennsylvania's Protect Our Games Act, introduced by state Sen. John Kane, which would require an offline mode, an online mode independent of company servers, or a minimum 25 percent refund when titles are shut down.

In a separate story, The Verge reported that Carolyn Marvin was arrested in Philadelphia and charged with disorderly conduct after blocking an Uber delivery robot and refusing to move. She told ABC13 she has protested the robots because she believes they take jobs from human delivery workers. Police asked her to move and handcuffed her when she did not. The incident was captured on video. The Verge said the robots are common in downtown Philadelphia and have drawn backlash, and that one was kicked over in Center City earlier this year.

Four people were killed and dozens seriously injured in a fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta, Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Sunday. He described a "violent, fast-moving" blaze and called it "one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime." He asked for flags on federal buildings to be flown at half-mast.

The cause has not been stated. The Department of National Defence said it is under investigation and that there were no indications of terrorism. The BBC reported that local media suggested a gas main may have been struck during a live firing exercise, but authorities have not confirmed this. Defence Minister David McGuinty said those caught in the fire were training on the range, and the RCMP is involved in the investigation. The fire was reported in the late afternoon on Saturday. The local municipal district said high winds spread it quickly across the base fence. No evacuation order was in effect.

Carney confirmed four deaths, all service members. The BBC said Canadian media had earlier reported seven dead, citing unnamed military sources. Carney did not say whether he expects the toll to rise, and the names of the dead have not been released. Wainwright's health facilities were overwhelmed, and patients were taken to Edmonton. Alberta's health service said its emergency response lasted 10 hours and involved 22 ambulances and eight aircraft. It expects care for the injured to be intensive.

Carney said he had asked military officials for a detailed account, and the defence department was expected to give reporters a technical briefing. The armed forces said their immediate priority was notifying next of kin and helping those affected. Alberta Premier Danielle Smith and Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre offered condolences and support.

French President Emmanuel Macron condemned the "unbridled violence" that followed one of the worst days of urban unrest in France in years. In a televised address on Sunday, he said rioters and looters would "pay for their crimes." He said local officials could ban certain street gatherings if they judged it necessary. Al Jazeera reported that he spoke of "anger and shame." The reports did not describe a curfew or state of emergency being announced.

Figures differ by outlet. Al Jazeera, citing the Interior Ministry, reported nearly 2,400 arrests on Saturday and about 1,000 police and gendarmes injured. The Guardian reported more than 2,000 arrests and about 600 police, firefighters and paramedics hurt. Police said a record 855 people were arrested in Paris. Traders' unions said more than 1,500 shops and businesses were ransacked.

Macron drew a line between peaceful demonstrators with "legitimate demands" and those who "destroy, ransack and loot." The Guardian said tens of thousands marched calmly on Saturday over school conditions and the cost of living. Macron blamed "factious groups from the ultra-left, joined by numerous delinquents." He promised a crisis unit and said lessons would be learned.

Reaction was sharp. Jean-Luc Melenchon said the government was "solely responsible" and had failed to organise public order. Jordan Bardella called the speech "lamentable" and "cowardly." The Guardian reported politicians on the left and right calling for Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez to resign. The Limoges mayor spoke of a "colossal failure of the state." Clashes flared again in Paris on Sunday, with police using teargas and stun grenades. Presidential elections are due next year, and Al Jazeera said the unrest is becoming a political football.

Protests in Tirana reached a sixth consecutive day on Sunday as Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama, in his fourth term, ruled out resigning. Al Jazeera reported that hundreds gathered outside the Ministry of Education chanting "Rama, resign." Police later used rubber bullets, water cannons and tear gas to hold back the crowds.

Protesters are demanding better education, more jobs, an end to alleged corruption and Rama's resignation. According to local media reports cited by Al Jazeera, demonstrators mainly targeted government institutions and police, including the Ministry of Education building and the area around Rama's office. Shops in the city centre have fitted metal shutters, and city workers removed paving stones so protesters could not use them.

Rama said in a live social media stream that "the government is not being challenged." He implied the unrest could affect Albania's path toward European Union membership, asking, "Do they want this, or do they want the EU?" Albania hopes to achieve membership status by 2030. He has blamed a "foreign hand" for the protests and said his government is doing its best to address corruption. He also said he was ready to listen to students' justified demands and discuss education costs, but that those responsible for destruction must be held accountable.

Albania's Ministry of Health said 65 people were injured on the latest day, 37 of them police officers, with 12 hospitalised. Since Tuesday, 272 people have been injured, including 169 officers. Analyst Mentor Nazarko told Al Jazeera that Rama's "legitimacy has melted away." TV Klan journalist Lindita Karadaku said both Rama and the young protesters are determined, and that no one knows what tomorrow will bring. Al Jazeera noted that discontent has built for months, starting with May protests against a luxury tourist project.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on NBC's Meet the Press on Sunday that he wants to trust President Donald Trump and hopes he will change his decisions. Zelenskyy called those decisions "mistakes" that "will not help us" or the United States. He thanked the Trump administration for resuming intelligence sharing on incoming Russian ballistic missiles, which he said Ukraine did not receive during three days of attacks.

Zelenskyy also said the US had intentionally limited Starlink speeds in Ukraine as a "message." He said SpaceX technically carried it out. The Guardian reported that this hampered drone operations and some air defence missions. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, on NBC, called the charge "reckless." He said Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio had "categorically" said no one in the administration did it.

The Guardian said Trump has sought a detente with Moscow, signing a deal to import Russian diesel and waiving sanctions that Congress passed by large margins. Zelenskyy said he spoke with envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and that communication with the administration is "virtually nonstop."

The fighting continues. Ukraine said it used more than 1,000 drones against Russian targets overnight, including in St Petersburg, and Russia said it downed 1,015. The Guardian reported that Trump's "energy ceasefire" collapsed within days, with each side resuming strikes. Lithuania told residents to shelter after an unidentified object entered its airspace. Ukraine's foreign ministry later said its drones may have strayed, possibly because of Russian electronic warfare, and apologised.

Ukraine hit St Petersburg in an overnight drone attack that killed at least one person, according to the BBC. St Petersburg governor Alexander Beglov said fires were being put out at the St Petersburg Oil Terminal and the Ruchyi oil depot, and at least five people were injured. Twelve apartment buildings and two homes were damaged, and Pulkovo Airport was temporarily closed.

The attack also hit technology and retail sites. VK, the Russian social network, confirmed a drone targeted its regional data centre but said services were available "as usual" after users reported outages. Ozon, a Russian online retailer, said a drone started a fire at its local logistics centre. It said staff were evacuated and no one was hurt. Russia's defence ministry said it shot down more than 1,000 Ukrainian drones overnight. Kyiv had not commented when the BBC published.

The BBC said Ukraine had paused strikes on Russian oil facilities for three days after Donald Trump declared an "energy ceasefire" last week, while accusing Russia of continuing its attacks. Ukraine resumed strikes earlier this week, and the BBC reported that this drew Trump's criticism. Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia had targeted Ukraine's energy sector 76 times since the announcement.

The BBC reported that relations between Washington and Kyiv have frayed since the US agreed to import Russian diesel to try to lower US energy prices. Zelensky suggested the deal amounts to investing in Russia's war effort. On Sunday he said he had spoken with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and that teams were preparing next diplomatic steps. Both sides are striking energy infrastructure harder ahead of winter.

President Donald Trump has endorsed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of Israel's October 27 Knesset elections, saying that if Israel has the wrong leader the United States would have to do the work against Iran itself. Fox News reported that Trump posted the message on Sunday, calling it his "Complete and Total Endorsement" of Netanyahu and describing him as a "great warrior" and a "partner for peace."

Trump wrote that Netanyahu did not "wilt" under pressure and that this is the kind of partner the United States demands of Israel. "If Israel has the wrong leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," he wrote. Netanyahu replied on X, thanking Trump for the "tremendous support and the joint work" and saying, "Together, we will complete the mission." The Fox report did not include responses from Netanyahu's opponents.

Fox explained how the vote works. Israelis vote for party lists, and seats in the 120-seat Knesset are shared proportionally among parties clearing a 3.25 percent threshold. Afterward, President Isaac Herzog, who is not on the ballot, consults party leaders and assigns a Knesset member, usually the one best placed to form a coalition. That person must win the support of at least 61 members.

Fox cited forecasts showing Likud winning roughly 18 to 22 seats. It said a Netanyahu-aligned right-religious bloc is projected at about 49 to 51 seats in total, short of a majority. That would leave smaller parties and possible coalition partners with the balance of power, so the coalition talks after the vote may matter as much as the result.

Former President Barack Obama said on Sunday that the federal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar's citizenship is "appalling." He wrote on X that the Trump administration is targeting her over her political views, and said the matter "should outrage all Americans." Federal agents searched Omar's home on October 12. Fox News reported that investigators are examining whether Omar or her father committed fraud on immigration paperwork when she became a citizen.

Obama said Omar arrived in the US at age 12 and automatically became a citizen at 17 when her father was naturalized. He said investigators are pursuing an "unsubstantiated theory" that she was actually 18, which would have required a separate application. He also cited federal actions against New York's attorney general, a former FBI director and Federal Reserve members, warning that future presidents of either party could do the same.

The White House pushed back. Spokeswoman Lauren Bis said that, unlike Joe Biden, Trump "has not weaponized the Department of Justice against his political foes." Trump has denied involvement, saying the matter is up to the Justice Department, though he also called Omar "totally crooked." On Fox News on Saturday, border czar Tom Homan was asked whether she could be denaturalized and deported. He answered, "Of course," if evidence shows she lied during naturalization, adding that the process is long. He declined to discuss other allegations, saying that was a question for the FBI.

Omar, who became a citizen in 2000 according to her lawyers, calls the allegations baseless lies. Her attorneys said there is no legitimate basis to suggest she broke any law. The Guardian reported that her phone was seized and that more than a dozen subpoenas have been issued. Omar is on the ballot in the November midterms.

Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed faced scrutiny on two fronts this weekend. Fox News reported that Morton Klein, president of the Zionist Organization of America, said El-Sayed's debate answer was a warning about elections after October 7. Klein said El-Sayed would not call Iran a bigger threat to the US than Israel. He said he spoke for himself, not for the organization.

According to Klein, El-Sayed said both countries are dangerous to America and called Israel as evil as Hamas. The Fox report did not include El-Sayed's response to that claim. Klein criticized Democratic leaders for not condemning El-Sayed, Rep. Ilhan Omar and others, and noted that Senator Elissa Slotkin and Attorney General Dana Nessel have endorsed El-Sayed. Fox noted that El-Sayed has called Judaism "a light unto the world" and said his commitment to Jewish safety equals his commitment to the safety of his own daughters.

Separately, the Guardian reported that CBS chief legal correspondent Jan Crawford deleted and apologized for a post about a Saturday town hall. A man identified as Tommy asked El-Sayed, "Will you disavow the Muslim Brotherhood?" El-Sayed answered, "Sure. Yeah, absolutely," then asked why the question was being posed. He said it implied he would have "dual loyalties." Crawford's post praised the questioner. She wrote that it violated CBS News standards.
Journalists and commentators criticized the post, and the Guardian cited internal backlash at CBS. El-Sayed faces Republican Mike Rogers in the November 3 election.
